Robert E. Lee. The commanding general of the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia and the most celebrated military figure of the American Civil War. Though his brilliant tactical maneuvers and inspired leadership of the South's best-equipped army prolonged the war and won him the devotion of his soldiers, his ultimate defeat by Ulysses S. Grant marked the end of the Confederacy and slavery in America. His legacy remains contested: celebrated by the South as a noble warrior defending his homeland, condemned by critics as the military arm of the slaveholding rebellion.

Born in Virginia in eighteen hundred seven into an old planter aristocracy, Lee graduated from West Point and served with distinction in the Mexican-American War, establishing himself as one of the United States Army's most promising officers. He turned down Lincoln's offer to command the Union armies, instead accepting command of Virginia's forces and eventually the Confederacy's principal army, the Army of Northern Virginia.

Lee won a series of stunning tactical victories despite being consistently outnumbered. He succeeded at the Second Battle of Bull Run in eighteen sixty-two, at Chancellorsville in eighteen sixty-three—his greatest victory despite the loss of his trusted subordinate Stonewall Jackson—and in the Peninsula Campaign. He invaded the North twice: after Antietam in eighteen sixty-two and leading to Gettysburg in eighteen sixty-three, attempting to bring the war to Union territory and secure European recognition for the Confederacy. Both invasions were repulsed.

Lee fought the defensive Siege of Petersburg from eighteen sixty-four to eighteen sixty-five for nearly a year against Grant's overwhelming numbers, demonstrating tactical mastery in the face of inevitable attrition. He surrendered at Appomattox Court House to Ulysses S. Grant in April eighteen sixty-five, effectively ending the war. He treated his defeated army with dignity and counseled reconciliation afterward. After the war, he served as president of Washington College, now Washington and Lee University, declining further military positions and working toward sectional healing.
